_sources.usda: USDA FoodData Central, https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/ (record named in each entry), read 2026-10-27
_sources.nihOds: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements fact sheets (Iron, Folate, Vitamin C, Vitamin K, Magnesium, Zinc, Potassium, Vitamin A, Calcium, Vitamin B12, Vitamin D, Vitamin E), https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/list-all/; reference intakes as listed in build_draft_batch.py (RDA for adult women)
_sources.niddk: NIDDK, Eating, Diet & Nutrition for Kidney Stones, read 2026-10-26: nuts and nut products, peanuts, rhubarb, spinach and wheat bran listed among foods to reduce for calcium oxalate stones

mushrooms.portion: 1 cup pieces or slices (USDA: 1 cup = 70 g)
mushrooms.offers: White (button) mushrooms are very low in energy and give potassium, along with a little protein.
mushrooms.how: Slice raw into salads, or sauté, roast or add to soups, omelettes and stir-fries. Cooking them in a dry pan first lets the water cook off so they brown.
mushrooms.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for mushrooms. They are a low-energy way to add bulk and potassium to a meal at any point in the cycle.
mushrooms.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
mushrooms.reviewNote: The catalogue entry covers button and shiitake; this is the white (button) mushroom record. Shiitake and others differ.
mushrooms.name: Mushrooms (button, shiitake)

brussels-sprouts.desc: Brussels sprouts, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt
brussels-sprouts.offers: Brussels sprouts are small cabbage-family buds that are rich in vitamin C and vitamin K, with some folate and fibre.
brussels-sprouts.how: Roast halved sprouts with olive oil until browned, shred them raw into slaws, or steam until just tender. Overcooking makes them bitter and sulphurous.
brussels-sprouts.cycle: Vitamin C helps your body absorb plant iron from the same meal (NIH ODS), so sprouts pair well with beans or lentils. No phase-specific claim is made.
brussels-sprouts.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
brussels-sprouts.name: Brussels sprouts

chard.desc: Chard, swiss, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt
chard.portion: ½ cup chopped, cooked (USDA: 1 cup = 175 g)
chard.offers: Swiss chard is a leafy green with plenty of vitamin A and vitamin K, magnesium, some vitamin C and a little plant iron.
chard.how: Sauté the leaves and stems separately, since the stems take longer. Stir the leaves into soups and eggs, or bake them into gratins with a squeeze of lemon.
chard.cycle: Iron needs are higher for women aged 19 to 50 (18 mg a day, against 8 mg for men), partly because of menstrual blood loss (NIH ODS). Chard adds some plant iron, which is absorbed less readily than iron from meat; vitamin C in the same meal helps.
chard.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
chard.name: Chard

eggplant.desc: Eggplant, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt
eggplant.portion: ½ cup cooked cubes (USDA: 1 cup of 1 in cubes = 99 g)
eggplant.offers: Eggplant is a mild, soft-textured vegetable that is very low in energy, with a little fibre and potassium. It is mostly valued for its texture rather than for concentrated nutrients.
eggplant.how: Roast or grill slices, blend into dips such as baba ganoush, or stew in curries and ratatouille. It soaks up oil when fried, so roasting or grilling uses less.
eggplant.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for eggplant. It is a low-energy vegetable that adds bulk and fibre to a meal at any time.
eggplant.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
eggplant.name: Eggplant

collard.desc: Collards, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt
collard.portion: ½ cup chopped, cooked (USDA: 1 cup = 190 g)
collard.offers: Collard greens are sturdy, slightly bitter leaves rich in vitamin A and vitamin K, with calcium, vitamin C and fibre.
collard.how: Simmer or braise until tender, shred into soups and stews, or use blanched leaves as wraps.
collard.cycle: Calcium needs are 1,000 mg a day for women aged 19 to 50 (NIH ODS). A half cup of cooked collards supplies about 13% of that, so it is a useful plant source; no phase-specific claim is made.
collard.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
collard.name: Collard

green-bell-pepper.offers: A green bell pepper is crisp and mild, and one medium pepper has about 96 mg of vitamin C, more than the 75 mg daily reference for adult women, plus a little potassium.
green-bell-pepper.how: Eat it raw in strips or salads, roast or stuff it, or sauté it in stir-fries and stews. Served with beans or lentils, its vitamin C helps your body absorb plant iron.
green-bell-pepper.cycle: Vitamin C improves the absorption of plant iron (NIH ODS), a useful pairing for anyone who menstruates and relies on plant foods for iron. No phase-specific claim is made.
green-bell-pepper.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
green-bell-pepper.name: Green bell pepper

white-potato.desc: Potatoes, baked, flesh and skin, without salt
white-potato.state: baked, flesh and skin, no salt
white-potato.portion: 1 medium baked potato with skin (USDA: 1 medium = 173 g)
white-potato.offers: A baked potato eaten with its skin is a filling starchy vegetable and a notable source of potassium (about 926 mg in a medium potato), with vitamin C, magnesium and fibre.
white-potato.how: Bake whole and eat with the skin, roast wedges, or boil and cool for potato salad. The USDA record is for flesh and skin together.
white-potato.cycle: Potassium has an adequate intake of 2,600 mg a day for women aged 19 to 50 (NIH ODS), and a medium baked potato supplies about 36% of it. No cycle-phase claim is made.
white-potato.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
white-potato.name: White potato

yellow-bell-pepper.offers: A yellow bell pepper is sweet and crunchy and exceptionally rich in vitamin C: ten strips supply about 96 mg, more than the 75 mg daily reference.
yellow-bell-pepper.how: Slice raw for snacking and salads, roast until soft and sweet, or grill. Add strips to a bean or lentil dish for extra vitamin C.
yellow-bell-pepper.cycle: Plant iron is absorbed better when vitamin C is in the same meal (NIH ODS); yellow pepper strips are an easy way to add it. No phase-specific claim is made.
yellow-bell-pepper.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
yellow-bell-pepper.name: Yellow bell pepper

lettuce.offers: Romaine is a crisp lettuce with a lot of vitamin A and folate for very few calories: two cups of shredded leaves give about 59% of the vitamin A and 32% of the folate reference, plus vitamin K.
lettuce.how: Use it as the base of salads, grill halves, or use the leaves as crunchy wraps. Dress it just before serving so it stays crisp.
lettuce.cycle: Folate is a nutrient some women of childbearing age do not get enough of (NIH ODS); leafy greens such as romaine are one source. No phase-specific claim is made.
lettuce.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
lettuce.reviewNote: The catalogue entry covers Bibb, Boston and romaine; this is the romaine record. Other lettuces differ.
lettuce.name: Lettuce (Bibb, Boston, romaine)

string-bean.desc: Beans, snap, green, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt
string-bean.offers: Green beans are crunchy, gently sweet pods with a little vitamin C, folate and vitamin K, and about 2 g of fibre in half a cup.
string-bean.how: Steam, blanch or sauté until bright green and just tender, then toss with garlic and lemon, or add to stir-fries and salads.
string-bean.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for green beans; they add fibre and some vitamin K to a meal at any point.
string-bean.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
string-bean.name: String bean

zucchini.desc: Squash, summer, zucchini, includes skin, raw
zucchini.offers: Zucchini is a mild summer squash, eaten with its skin, that is very low in energy and gives vitamin C and potassium.
zucchini.how: Slice or ribbon it raw into salads, grill, sauté or roast it, or grate it into fritters and baking.
zucchini.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for zucchini; it is a light vegetable for adding volume to a meal.
zucchini.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
zucchini.name: Zucchini

arugula.offers: Arugula (rocket) is a peppery salad leaf. Two cups give vitamin K, folate, calcium and some vitamin A for about 10 calories.
arugula.how: Toss it raw into salads, pile it onto pizza or pasta after cooking, or blend it into pesto. Its peppery bite softens when wilted.
arugula.cycle: Folate is a nutrient some women of childbearing age do not get enough of (NIH ODS), and leafy greens such as arugula contribute some. No cycle-phase claim is made.
arugula.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
arugula.name: Arugula (rocket)

bok-choy.desc: Cabbage, chinese (pak-choi), cooked, boiled, drained, without salt
bok-choy.portion: ½ cup shredded, cooked (USDA: 1 cup = 170 g)
bok-choy.offers: Bok choy is a mild, juicy Chinese cabbage with vitamin C, vitamin A and potassium, and a little calcium.
bok-choy.how: Halve or chop it and steam, stir-fry or add to noodle soups, giving the stems a minute's head start on the leaves.
bok-choy.cycle: Calcium needs are 1,000 mg a day for women aged 19 to 50 (NIH ODS). Cooked bok choy has about 93 mg of calcium per 100 g, so it is a modest contributor rather than a major source.
bok-choy.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
bok-choy.name: Bok choy

napa-cabbage.offers: Napa cabbage is a tender, mild cabbage with vitamin C and folate; a cup of shredded leaves has only about 12 calories.
napa-cabbage.how: Shred it raw into slaws and salads, stir-fry it, add it to soups, or ferment it into kimchi.
napa-cabbage.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for napa cabbage. It is a light, easy way to add vitamin C and folate to a meal.
napa-cabbage.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
napa-cabbage.name: Napa cabbage

turnip.desc: Turnips, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt
turnip.portion: ½ cup cubes, cooked (USDA: 1 cup cubes = 156 g)
turnip.offers: Turnips are a peppery root vegetable, low in energy, that give a little vitamin C, potassium and fibre.
turnip.how: Roast in wedges, boil and mash with or instead of potato, or add to soups and stews. Very small, young turnips can be eaten raw.
turnip.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for turnips; they are a modest source of vitamin C and potassium.
turnip.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
turnip.name: Turnip

asparagus.state: cooked, boiled, drained (USDA record is without added salt where stated; this record has none listed)
asparagus.portion: ½ cup cooked (USDA: 0.5 cup = 90 g), about 6 spears
asparagus.offers: Asparagus is a tender spring vegetable and a good source of folate (about 34% of the reference in half a cup), with vitamin K and vitamin C.
asparagus.how: Snap off the woody ends, then roast, grill or steam for a few minutes until just tender.
asparagus.cycle: Folate is a nutrient some women of childbearing age do not get enough of (NIH ODS); asparagus is one of the richer vegetable sources. No phase-specific claim is made.
asparagus.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
asparagus.name: Asparagus

celery.portion: 1 medium stalk (USDA: 1 stalk, 7½–8 in long = 40 g)
celery.offers: Celery is a crisp, watery stalk that is very low in energy; one stalk gives a little potassium, vitamin K and folate.
celery.how: Eat it raw with dips, slice it into salads and slaws, or use it as the aromatic base of soups and stews.
celery.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for celery.
celery.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
celery.name: Celery

radish.offers: Radishes are peppery, crunchy roots with some vitamin C and potassium for almost no energy.
radish.how: Slice raw into salads and sandwiches, serve with butter and salt, or roast to mellow their bite.
radish.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for radishes; they are a small source of vitamin C.
radish.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
radish.name: Radish

bean-sprouts.desc: Mung beans, mature seeds, sprouted, raw
bean-sprouts.offers: Mung bean sprouts are crisp and light, with some vitamin C and folate and about 1.6 g of protein in half a cup.
bean-sprouts.how: Add them to stir-fries and noodle dishes at the end of cooking, or to salads and spring rolls.
bean-sprouts.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for bean sprouts.
bean-sprouts.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
bean-sprouts.reviewNote: Catalogue "bean sprouts" is read as mung bean sprouts, the common kind. Raw sprouts carry a food-safety caution (FDA/USDA) that has not been added; see the editorial list.
bean-sprouts.name: Bean sprouts

red-cabbage.offers: Red cabbage is a crunchy, slightly peppery cabbage with plenty of vitamin C (about 53% of the reference in a cup of shredded leaves) and vitamin K.
red-cabbage.how: Shred raw into slaws, or braise slowly with apple and vinegar. A splash of vinegar keeps the colour bright.
red-cabbage.cycle: Vitamin C helps your body absorb plant iron (NIH ODS); a red cabbage slaw alongside beans or lentils is one pairing. No phase-specific claim is made.
red-cabbage.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
red-cabbage.name: Red cabbage

sugar-snap-peas.portion: 1 cup whole pods (USDA: 1 cup whole = 63 g)
sugar-snap-peas.offers: Sugar snap peas are sweet, crunchy edible pods with plenty of vitamin C (about half the daily reference in a cup) and a little plant iron.
sugar-snap-peas.how: Eat them raw as a snack or in salads, or stir-fry briefly so they stay crisp.
sugar-snap-peas.cycle: They add vitamin C and a little plant iron to the same meal, a pairing NIH ODS describes: vitamin C helps iron from plant foods be absorbed. No phase-specific claim is made.
sugar-snap-peas.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
sugar-snap-peas.name: Sugar snap peas

artichoke.desc: Artichokes, (globe or french), cooked, boiled, drained, without salt
artichoke.portion: 1 medium artichoke, cooked (USDA: 1 medium = 120 g, edible parts)
artichoke.offers: A cooked artichoke is a fibre-rich vegetable (about 6.8 g in one medium artichoke) with folate, magnesium and potassium.
artichoke.how: Steam or boil it whole until a leaf pulls out easily, dip the leaf bases in a sauce, and eat the heart. Canned or jarred hearts work in salads and pasta.
artichoke.cycle: Folate is a nutrient some women of childbearing age do not get enough of (NIH ODS); artichoke is a good source. No phase-specific claim is made.
artichoke.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
artichoke.name: Artichoke

parsnip.desc: Parsnips, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt
parsnip.portion: ½ cup slices, cooked (USDA: 0.5 cup = 78 g)
parsnip.offers: Parsnips are sweet, starchy roots with fibre, potassium, vitamin C and folate.
parsnip.how: Roast with a little oil until caramelised, simmer into soups, or mash with potato.
parsnip.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for parsnips; they add fibre, potassium and folate to a meal.
parsnip.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
parsnip.name: Parsnip

squash.desc: Squash, winter, all varieties, cooked, baked, without salt
squash.state: baked, no salt, all winter varieties
squash.portion: ½ cup cubes, baked (USDA: 1 cup cubes = 205 g)
squash.offers: Baked winter squash is a soft, sweet vegetable that supplies vitamin A (from carotenoids) and some vitamin C; half a cup gives about a third of the vitamin A reference.
squash.how: Roast it in wedges or cubes, scoop out baked halves, or purée it into soups and sauces.
squash.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for squash. Varieties differ, so these values are approximate.
squash.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
squash.reviewNote: The catalogue entry "squash" is not specific. This is the USDA record for winter squash, all varieties, baked; butternut, acorn and others vary.
squash.name: Squash
